html:
In May 1944, on Stalin's orders, the Soviet secret police deported the whole Crimean Tatar people, nearly 200,000 people, from Crimea to Central Asia, mostly to Uzbekistan, in about three days.

The Crimean Tatars were the native Muslim people of the peninsula, heirs of the Crimean Khanate, which Russia had annexed in 1783. After the Red Army took Crimea back from the Germans in 1944, the state accused the entire people of collaborating with the occupiers, though many had fought in the Red Army.

Families were given minutes to pack and were loaded into cattle wagons. Many died on the long journey, and many more of hunger and disease in the special settlements, where they had to stay under police watch. Estimates of the death toll range from about a fifth to nearly half of those deported. Their homes and lands in Crimea were given to newcomers.

The Volga Germans, Chechens and other peoples suffered similar deportations. Crimean Tatars were allowed to return only from the late 1980s. In 2015 Ukraine recognised the deportation as genocide. The same event appears on the chart as Crimean Tatars deported.
